name: Defynnog Yew

location.address: St Cynog's churchyard, Defynnog, Sennybridge, Powys LD3 8SE

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, Defynnog (Tim Hills, 1998)

access: Free. Open churchyard of St Cynog's, Defynnog, in the Brecon Beacons National Park.
transport: The TrawsCymru T6 bus between Brecon and Swansea stops in Defynnog (Lion Inn and Tanners Arms), roughly every two hours in the daytime; check the current timetable. No railway.

photo_candidate.author: Rosser1954
photo_candidate.why_this_trunk: file titled for the Defynnog Yew trees; more files in the same Commons set (bole, canopy, roots)

story:
A certificate signed by the botanist David Bellamy, kept at a café near this churchyard, says the great yew of Defynnog is about 5,000 years old. The people who have looked hardest are more cautious. Wikipedia reports that an investigation does not support the figure and calls 2,000 to 3,000 years more likely; one assessment gives 3,018. Toby Hindson of the Ancient Yew Group sets a minimum of 1,300 years, on the hard evidence the group holds. When the 5,000 figure reached the press in 2014, it came with the label of Britain's oldest tree. That is a claim several Welsh yews make, and we make it for none of them.

What is not disputed is the size. The tree grows from a mound about eight metres across and a metre high, as nine stems with a combined girth of about 11 metres. A second, smaller yew about five metres west has been shown by DNA to be genetically identical, possibly grown from a drooping branch that touched the ground and rooted. Two more ancient yews stand on the south side, and those are not clones.

The church of St Cynog is mostly Norman and 15th century, and its porch holds a stone inscribed in both ogham and Latin. Graves have been dug between the two northern yews. Look closely at the smaller tree and you may find a small patch of albino leaves among the green.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the nine stems rising from a low mound about eight metres across, north of the church. A smaller yew stands about five metres west of it, its genetic twin.

name: Discoed Yew

location.address: St Michael's churchyard, Discoed, Presteigne, Powys LD8 2NR

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, Discoed (Tim Hills, 1998)

access: Free. Open churchyard of St Michael's, Discoed.
transport: No railway and no regular bus. Discoed is about 5 km west of Presteigne, a short drive or an hour's walk.
story:
Popular opinion in this corner of Radnorshire makes the Discoed yew the oldest in Wales, some 5,000 years old. The figure goes back to Allen Meredith's graphs relating a yew's size to its age, and the monument guide Wondermondo, which repeats it, is careful to add that no one knows this for sure and that it is most likely not true. Several other Welsh yews carry rival claims. We back none of them.

The tree itself needs no exaggeration. The Ancient Yew Group measured it at 9.68 metres round, 90 centimetres up, in 1998; another figure in circulation is 11.28 metres, and a 1994 gazetteer put it at 22 feet. Yews this hollow and irregular are hard to measure the same way twice. It stands north of the small church of St Michael, first mentioned in 1291, with a second ancient yew in the same churchyard, 6.71 metres round, and a third notable one by the lane to the car park. A spring at the churchyard gate has become a well.

Nobody has dated the tree in a way that settles anything, so we give it no age. Our most recent record of it is not recent either, so if you visit St Michael's, tell us how it is doing and send a photograph.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the giant yew north of the church, the larger of the two ancient yews in the churchyard. It stands in St Michael's churchyard, Discoed; a smaller notable yew is by the car-park lane.

name: Pennant Melangell Yews

location.address: St Melangell's Church, Pennant Melangell, Llangynog, Powys SY10 0HQ

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, Pennant Melangell (Tim Hills, 1998)

access: Free. Open churchyard of St Melangell's shrine church, at the end of a remote Berwyn valley road.
transport: No railway or bus to the church. Buses reach Llangynog from Oswestry (check Traveline Cymru); from there it is about 4 miles (6 km) up the valley road on foot.

photo_candidate.author: Rosser1954
photo_candidate.why_this_trunk: file titled ancient yew tree, St Melangell's Church

story:
Burial pits found at this church site have been carbon-dated to between 1500 and 1000 BC, so the round churchyard at Pennant Melangell was a burial ground long before any yew we can see here. Today it is ringed by them. Six yews grow around the circular wall, four of them ancient, the largest 8.71 metres round at its narrowest point.

The church at the centre is the 12th-century shrine of St Melangell, at the head of a dead-end valley in the Berwyn hills. Her legend says she sheltered a hunted hare under her cloak and faced down a prince and his hounds, which is why she is the patron saint of hares, and why pilgrims still come up this valley.

The church says its yews are estimated to be 2,000 years old, and the National Churches Trust gives the same figure. Both are estimates rather than measurements. Others are more cautious, noting that certificates have dated some Welsh yews to only 500 to 800 years, so treat 2,000 as the church's figure and the honest range as wide.

Come for the ring rather than one trunk. The yews, the circular wall and the small shrine church make one place to stand, and an observer for the Ancient Yew Group, visiting in 2008, called it a memorable site. Four miles up a lane from Llangynog, it is not a place you pass on the way to anywhere.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the yews ringing the circular churchyard wall, the largest 8.71 metres round. They stand around St Melangell's shrine church at the head of the valley above Llangynog.

name: Llanerfyl Yew

location.address: St Erfyl's churchyard, Llanerfyl, Welshpool, Powys SY21 0EN

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, Llanerfyl (Tim Hills, 1998)

access: Free. Open churchyard of St Erfyl's, Llanerfyl.
transport: Llanerfyl is on the A458 west of Welshpool, about 30 minutes by car. Buses along the A458 are few; check Traveline Cymru before relying on one.

photo_candidate.file_page: geograph (Dave Croker and John Firth photos used by Wondermondo, CC BY-SA 2.0, file page not located)
photo_candidate.author: Dave Croker / John Firth
photo_candidate.why_this_trunk: Wondermondo credits them for St Erfyl's Church and the Llanerfyl Yew; Commons file page not yet found

story:
What looks like four yews standing in a circle is reported to be a single tree. The trunks at St Erfyl's measure 10.67 metres around all four together, and DNA work is said to show they are one organism, even though three of the stems are recorded as female and one as male.

It has been admired for a long time. Lewis's Topographical Dictionary of Wales called it one of the finest yew-trees in the principality, and an account of 1872 named it the mother yew of Montgomeryshire. Its legend is older still. St Padarn is said to have left his staff, Cyrwen, here in the late sixth or early seventh century, and the yew grew from it.

The ground beneath it held something real. In 1915 a stone inscribed in the fifth or sixth century was taken from under the tree, and it is now on display inside the church. A low wall circles the yew today.

The age you will see quoted, about 1,400 years, rests on the legend and on a blog rather than any measurement, so we call it ancient and leave the number open. If you know of better evidence, tell us. Llanerfyl is a small village on the A458 west of Welshpool, and the churchyard is the reason to stop.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its four trunks standing in a ring inside a low wall. It stands in St Erfyl's churchyard in the centre of Llanerfyl.

name: Gresford Yew
age_estimate: ancient, older than the 13th-century church (Ancient Yew Group); no measured age

location.address: All Saints' churchyard, Church Street, Gresford, Wrexham LL12 8RG

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, Gresford (Tim Hills, 1999)

access: Free. Open churchyard of All Saints', Gresford.
transport: Buses between Wrexham and Chester stop in Gresford, a short walk from the church; check the operator's timetable. Gresford no longer has a railway station.

photo_candidate.author: John S Turner
photo_candidate.why_this_trunk: title 'Ancient yew at All Saints', Gresford'

story:
The Seven Wonders of Wales rhyme remembers Gresford for its church bells. It could have picked the yew. The Ancient Yew Group says the Gresford Yew is certainly older than the 13th-century fabric of All Saints', and it measured the trunk at 8.99 metres round in 1999.

It does not stand alone. The churchyard holds 33 younger yews, and the church lists them among its remarkable features. Wikipedia's account of the church says this one was already an ancient tree when Richard II ordered yews planted for longbows, which would make it old in the 14th century.

Everything else about its age is guesswork, and we would rather say so. No one has published a measured age, and the round numbers you may hear are not ones we can trace. Ancient is the honest word, and the 13th-century church is the firmest clue.

It was already an old tree when the Gresford colliery disaster of 1934 killed 266 men underground.

The churchyard is open. Find the biggest of the yews; at nearly nine metres round, it is not hard.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, nearly nine metres round, far bigger than any of the 33 younger yews around it. It stands in All Saints' churchyard, Gresford.

name: Bleeding Yew of Nevern
age_estimate: not documented, the avenue is put at roughly 600 to 700 years

location.address: St Brynach's churchyard, Nevern, Newport, Pembrokeshire SA42 0NF

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, Nevern (Tim Hills, 1999)

access: Free. Open churchyard of St Brynach's, Nevern.
transport: No railway. Nevern is about 3 km east of Newport, Pembrokeshire; buses on the Fishguard to Cardigan road pass the turning, check Traveline Cymru. The coastal Poppit Rocket runs in summer.
story:
The second yew on the right as you walk up to St Brynach's church weeps a dark red-brown sap from a broken stub, and thousands of people come every year to see it. The Ancient Yew Group is blunt about the avenue it stands in. These yews are of no great age, it says, and are on its list only because of the bleeding one.

Why it bleeds is the question the Pembrokeshire Coast National Park asks on its own page about the tree, along with when it will stop. Legend has its answers. One links it to the Crucifixion. Another says it will bleed until a Welsh prince rules again from Nevern Castle, on the hill above the village.

The churchyard has older witnesses than the tree. A carved Celtic cross dates from the late tenth or early eleventh century, and the Vitalianus stone, inscribed in Latin and ogham, stands nearby. The church itself was built around 1380 on the site of St Brynach's early foundation.

The avenue is sometimes put at 600 to 700 years, a figure we could not trace to a firm source, and nobody has recorded this tree's girth. If you can add either, tell us.

Nothing else in the churchyard looks like it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the dark red sap running from a broken stub on its trunk. It is the second yew on the right of the avenue leading to the church door at St Brynach's.
